summary: Specifies procedures for using bidirectional tunnels as provider tunnels in multicast VPNs for BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, extending earlier procedures for carrying customer multicast data through a provider backbone.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7582 fills in how bidirectional tunnels carry multicast traffic across a provider network for customer VPNs. It defines how routers advertise tunnel choices and how receiving routers identify the expected path, with partitioned methods for distinguishing traffic and an unpartitioned method with less identification detail.

questions: what is the pmsi tunnel attribute
subtitle: Defines how bidirectional provider tunnels carry multicast traffic for BGP/MPLS VPNs.

tldr.problem: Earlier multicast VPN specifications named bidirectional provider tunnels but did not fully define how customer multicast flows use and identify them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines procedures for assigning flows to tunnels, advertising the assignments through BGP, and deciding which tunnel should carry or receive each flow.
tldr.outcome: Providers can use bidirectional tunnels for customer multicast traffic, choosing between partitioned and unpartitioned methods with different state and identification trade-offs.

today: RFC 7582 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFCs 6513, 6514, and 6625.

sections.title: Bidirectional Tunnels for Multicast VPNs
sections.content:
Multicast VPNs use provider tunnels to carry customer multicast traffic between provider-edge routers. Earlier RFCs defined tunnel identifiers and BGP advertisement formats, but left some procedures for bidirectional tunnels outside their scope.

RFC 7582 supplies procedures to assign customer flows to bidirectional provider tunnels, advertise those assignments, and determine which tunnel a flow should use. The customer flow itself may be unidirectional or bidirectional.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC explains how a provider network carries customer multicast flows over bidirectional tunnels. It adds the rules for advertising tunnel assignments and matching traffic to the right tunnel.

sections.title: Supported Tunnel Technologies
sections.content:
The specification covers two bidirectional tunnel technologies: Multipoint-to-Multipoint Label Switched Paths (MP2MP LSPs) built with LDP extensions, and multicast distribution trees built with BIDIR-PIM.

The provider advertises the tunnel through a Provider Multicast Service Interface (PMSI) Tunnel attribute attached to BGP auto-discovery routes. Other bidirectional tunnel technologies and some combinations of tunnel type and instantiation method are outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC supports MP2MP label-switched paths and BIDIR-PIM trees. BGP advertisements tell other provider-edge routers which provider tunnel represents a multicast service.

sections.title: Three Ways to Instantiate a PMSI
sections.content:
The Flat Partitioned Method uses a set of separate bidirectional tunnels. Each tunnel has a distinguished provider-edge router, and receiving routers can identify that router from the tunnel the packet arrived on.

The Hierarchical Partitioned Method aggregates inner tunnels under an outer tunnel and uses provider-edge distinguisher labels, reducing state in transit routers. The Unpartitioned Method uses one or more shared bidirectional tunnels but does not identify which provider-edge router sent each received packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Partitioned methods let receiving routers identify a packet's distinguished provider-edge router. Hierarchical partitioning can reduce tunnel state in the network core, while unpartitioned tunneling uses simpler shared paths without that sender distinction.

sections.title: Matching Flows to Tunnels
sections.content:
Provider-edge routers use BGP auto-discovery routes and their tunnel attributes to decide which tunnel matches a customer multicast flow for transmission or reception. Selective PMSIs can match particular flows or wildcard groups; an inclusive PMSI carries traffic not assigned to a selective one.

With partitioning, a receiving router checks that the packet arrived with the expected distinguished provider-edge identity and discards it otherwise. The Unpartitioned Method cannot use that same distinction, so its procedures treat packets received on any advertised tunnel as belonging to the inclusive service.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers match each customer multicast flow against BGP advertisements to choose a tunnel. Partitioned tunnels also let a receiver check which provider-edge router the flow should be associated with.

sections.title: Minimum Support and Security
sections.content:
Bidirectional tunnel support is optional. An implementation that offers it must support at least one of the two specified tunnel technologies and an allowed instantiation method.

An implementation that provides customer bidirectional multicast using partitioned sets must support at least the flat partial-mesh method described by the RFC. The security considerations remain those of the underlying multicast VPN and tunnel protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers do not have to implement bidirectional tunnels. If they do, the RFC defines the minimum tunnel technology and procedures needed to claim compliance.
